item.title: We Listen with Four Ears, with a Whole Inner Team
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

We Listen with Four Ears, with a Whole Inner Team

Insights from communication psychology for a good life.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • German psychologist Friedemann Schulz von Thun’s communication models have helped millions of people.
  • With one sentence, we are delivering and hearing four different messages.
  • We can harness the different voices in our head, our inner team, for better outcomes.
  • A magnanimous way of relating to our inner plurality is an ideal way of relating to ourselves.

“What we speak becomes the house we live in.” These words, attributed to the 14th-century poet Hafez, could be a modern dictum of a good life. What we speak—the words we string together day after day, silently or stridently, to ourselves or to others—is how we communicate. Yet communication is hardly the first thing that comes to mind when we consider well-being. It’s one of those automatic practices we perform out of necessity, often mindlessly, with varying success.

This mundane activity may be far more consequential than we realize.

Maybe with our words, we capture the evanescence of thought and share our worlds, but also lay the ground for our very happiness.

Friedemann Schulz von Thun, an eminent scholar of communication psychology, has helped millions understand themselves and others better. As Bernhard Poerksen, professor of media studies at the University of Tübingen, has written, Schulz von Thun has “revolutionized and revived” humanistic psychology and is “probably the most widely read psychologist in the German‐speaking world.” Humans, Schulz von Thun says, are “both-and beings” who have both “roots and wings” and need both “self-care and dedication to the whole.” For lasting happiness, he writes, hedonic (pleasure) and eudaimonic (meaning) fulfillment must be in balance. The good life, for him, lies in tolerating these tensions and integrating opposites—welcoming the conflicting emotions within us, and those we encounter when communing with the world.

His latest book, Communication As An Art of Living (2026), co-authored with Poerksen, is an ode to communication as an unexpected, inspiring facet of a good life.

Here are two of Schulz von Thun’s models that can transform how we think about communication, with others and with ourselves.

Communication Square

Schulz von Thun notes that communication plays out on four fields at once. Utter one sentence and you deliver four different messages: information (factual content), something about yourself (self-disclosure), your thoughts and attitudes about your interlocutor (relationship), and something that you want to achieve (appeal).

The authors consider the following example.

A woman is driving a car when the man next to her in the passenger seat exclaims, “Hey, green light up ahead!” This sentence reveals information about the traffic situation; however, the tone also discloses something about the speaker (perhaps he is in a hurry), his relationship with the woman (perhaps he is unhappy with her driving skills), and even an appeal (perhaps to drive faster).

Source: Copyright: Friedemann Schulz von Thun

While the speaker sends four possible messages (“speaks with four beaks,” in Schulz von Thun’s words), the listener hears the message “with four ears.” For example, as the authors write, if someone has the habit of listening with the “relationship” ear, they risk taking every verbal and non-verbal signal as a barometer of the state of their connection. In this mode, we take things personally, and words can be received as insults. But if ears are switched, it's possible to hear something about the person—say, their pain—which can dampen the listener’s reactiveness and defensiveness.

“May the communication square make you more aware of the simultaneity of what is going on, complete with a feel for the four levels and the ability to deliberately switch levels in difficult moments, for which you should have all four beaks and four ears at your disposal,” writes Schulz von Thun.

Inner Team

If communication between two brains comes with obvious challenges, one might expect things to run more smoothly within a single mind. Alas, the picture is just as complex there. Our “inner plurality,” as Schulz von Thun calls it, can cause inner strife, since the different voices in our heads seem to have their own needs, wants, and agendas. Say we have a goal to accomplish: The optimistic cheerleader offers encouragement; the fearful voice offers a hundred reasons to stand down; the critical one reminds us of our flaws and casts doubts on our abilities; the social one weighs the goal’s repercussions for our reputation.

What do we do when faced with these loud, sometimes confrontational, often incompatible inner voices?

Schulz von Thun’s epiphany was to “make virtue of necessity,” to harness these diverse perspectives to achieve an even better outcome.

The “inner team” metaphor was born.

This “human energy reservoir” of inner voices, he says, requires leadership. As a guiding star, he chose higher-order harmony, the idea that differences are not merely allowed to co-exist but welcomed. The first step in this self-leadership is to recognize these inner voices and to “take their concerns seriously.” A magnanimous way of relating to our inner plurality, he says, is an ideal way of relating to ourselves.

“Welcome everybody however they want to come, also and especially those that may run counter to your ideal self! Assume that they are well-intentioned and that their opinion contains at least a kernel of truth that wants to be noticed and that will still be needed.”

Once each voice has had its say, the next step is an “internal heart-to-heart,” in which the individual arrives at “self-clarification.” The team captain moderates and integrates the voices, reaching a collective answer that everyone can accept.

Source: Graphicmama Team on Pixabay

Schulz von Thun offers an example of the inner team leader having an “appreciating interview” with the inner perfectionist, who, by fearing mediocrity and demanding 100 percent excellence, is keeping him from trying new things.

“Dear Perfectionist, I know you mean well and want what’s best for me; but sometimes you go too far in your good intentions and make things difficult for me! Would you mind telling me when you first emerged, why you were needed back then, and what’s on your mind now? And why are you so afraid of average performance? Once heard and appreciated, the perfectionist can relax and become more open to his boss’s requests.”

This benevolent attitude has numerous advantages, says Schulz von Thun. Everyone gets heard, so no overlooked voice looks for later revenge. Self-contempt is absent: kindness is shown to all, and nobody is exiled. Reaching an agreement with ourselves makes us better communicators, because we can “face the world with combined forces.” The resulting solution is more “authentic” and “appropriate” when every perspective is accounted for. And finally, and perhaps most importantly, once all are welcomed— there is the coveted inner peace, the centerpiece of a good life—that suddenly becomes accessible.

Many thanks to Friedemann Schulz von Thun and Bernhard Poerksen for their time and insights. Friedemann Schulz von Thun is a bestselling author and Professor Emeritus at the University of Hamburg, Germany. Bernhard Poerksen is Professor of Media Studies at the University of Tübingen, Germany.

item.title: The Beauty of Being All of You
item.description:
Wisdom

The Beauty of Being All of You

Accepting the advantage of imperfection

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Imperfection is not a concession; it’s an absolute.
  • We have to be open to our imperfections as something to paradoxically strive for, not as something to avoid.
  • To live authentically, we have to unite the positive aspects of ourselves with the allegedly negative parts.

What if I told you that resisting your imperfect uniqueness goes against not only who you are intrinsically, but also goes against the natural order of being human? Sounds strange, right? But it’s not.

For example, the Japanese philosophy called wabi-sabi, the art of paying homage to the elegance of imperfection, instructs us to do a “180” and reexamine our socialized inclination to do things the “right” way. In other words, to always strive for perfection. Perfection is, at best, an abstract, an illusion. However, imperfection is not, because it’s the natural state of all things. Imperfection is not a concession; it’s an absolute.

One of the goals of wabi-sabi is to transform our perception of defectiveness into aspects we can celebrate and seek out. Wabi-sabi is a design for living that is magnificently contradictory. It motivates us to embrace our faulty uniqueness and even draw attention to it. It inspires us to highlight our distinctiveness even when others don’t. The beauty is in the paradox.

The Wisdom of Unquestioned Design

Think about it: The beauty of the natural world is essentially flawed, but we never judge it. It just is. Consequently, looking deeper into nature for illustrations of astounding imperfection helps to create more insight. It becomes a portal of inspiration where we convert criticism into curiosity and wonderment. It dilates our pupils of understanding.

Did you know that about 71 percent of Earth’s surface is covered in seawater? Additionally, only about 3 percent of it is freshwater. Most of it is inaccessible to human use, frozen in remote ice caps and glaciers. Hence, less than 1 percent of Earth’s water is drinkable. Even though those numbers are mind-boggling and seemingly ill-designed by an intelligent universe or a creator, we don’t question it.

On land, there are plenty of beauteous imperfections as well. For instance, the weathered rocks of the Earth, with their cracks, fissures, and rough textures, are not defects but wear-and-tear symbols of resilience and adaptation. They are majestic imprints of time and endurance that even predate the evolution of our human species. The mountains and landscapes, with their inconsistent terrains, rugged surfaces, and even our colliding tectonic plates, are all curiously exquisite as well.

The same can be said of the diverse, wide-ranging climates and changing seasons. Extreme environments can be found in all areas of the planet, some more inhospitable than others, yet we are humbled by them. We don’t seek inquiry; we just defer to its splendor. Our planet is our home. It’s all we have, and over the millennia, we have grown to respect it and admire it with awe.

Therefore, the philosophy of wabi-sabi reassures us that, like the natural world, recognizing our imperfections is a plus.

The Tyranny of Perfectionism

Author and researcher Brené Brown, who calls herself a “recovering perfectionist,” says “perfectionism is the belief that if we live perfect, look perfect and act perfect, we can minimize or avoid the pain of blame, judgment and shame.” Hence, we develop a dependence on trying to do things right all the time, saying the right thing, or trying to succeed at everything at all costs. We are blinded to the compassionate tenets of imperfection. We have to be open to our imperfections as something to paradoxically strive for, not as something to avoid. But we are so conditioned to react apologetically to it that it's easier said than done. “Where perfectionism exists, shame is always lurking. In fact, shame is the birthplace of perfectionism,” says Brown.

She also says we have to regularly identify the shame that is “always lurking,” and mentor ourselves not to let shame drive the bus. We can let go of the struggle that often leaves us rejecting our true selves. But like most pivotal changes in life, it will not happen overnight.

Here’s one reason why:

Most human beings are prone to lean into “results orientation” as opposed to “process orientation.” Results orientation is when we are stuck in a loop of always desiring quick solutions, seamless answers, and being “right.” It makes us impatient and easily annoyed, which sometimes leads to poor decision-making. It reacts from a place of fear and distrust, and its holy grail is achieving exactness. Results orientation forces us to judge our self-worth only by our successes or lack thereof. In a word, results orientation is oppressive. It’s rigid and rejects our flawed uniqueness by always seeking perfection.

“Process orientation,” on the other hand, is guided by patience and wisdom and understands that temperance is more effective than impulsivity. There are no quick fixes to anything. It is not concerned with seeking exactness and understands the power of gradual change. It helps us to see that building self-worth is a progression that takes time, effort, and determination. Process orientation values human mistakes as learning experiences and can see the virtue in the limitations of life. Process orientation believes in “failing forward,” not backward. It understands that growing and evolving means integrating all aspects of being human, even our misgivings.

In her 2024 book, High Functioning Anxiety, Dr. Lalitaa Suglani delved into the profiles of otherwise confident people who suffered bouts of excessive worry, fear of failure, and, most importantly, not feeling “good enough.” People with HFA are praised for their fortitude and tenacity; they are relied upon to get things done and always appear to be balanced and in control. But deep down inside, they are often churning and tend to reject the imperfect sides of themselves.

Consequently, she says that to live authentically, we have to unite the positive aspects of ourselves with the allegedly negative parts. She writes, “To integrate the two sides of you—your learned side and your shadow side—you need to face the shadow.” The shadow she speaks of is perhaps the idiosyncrasies that you have labeled as undesirable. So, embrace your imperfect self and see the beauty and the peace in it.

item.title: Why Do People Miss Drinking Even When They Want to Quit?
item.description:
Alcoholism

Why Do People Miss Drinking Even When They Want to Quit?

How a 'Near Enemy Trap' may keep us stuck with the desire to drink.

Posted September 16, 2026

“I know alcohol is bad for me, but why do I still miss it so much?”

If you are trying to quit drinking, there is a good chance that you recognize this feeling.

I have worked with many people who feel puzzled, or even embarrassed, about continuing to miss alcohol after they decide to quit. They feel like the FOMO they feel when they turn down a drink is an indication that they are too weak, and the lingering craving is a sign that something is wrong with them. So if you feel that way too, you are not alone.

My goal in this post is to help you see that there is a reason that you still miss alcohol, and that it is not because there is something wrong with you.

The Invisible Drinking Loop
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

What do people really want when they say “I miss alcohol”?

Here is the thing that many people don’t realize: when a person says “I miss alcohol,” it’s rarely alcohol itself that they miss. More often than not, what the person really longs for are the things that alcohol has come to represent in their life. For many people, this could look like:

  • A boost of confidence
  • A shortcut into connection
  • Or a gateway into good times

Beneath these desires are fundamental human needs: to feel secure in ourselves, to feel connected and accepted by others, and to experience joy and enjoyment in life. In what I call the Invisible Drinking Loop, these unnamed needs are the first core invisible force that keeps pulling a person back to an unwanted drinking pattern.

We believe alcohol helps us get what we want

Of course, need alone doesn’t create the desire to drink. It’s when an unnamed need meets the belief that alcohol can help with that need that the desire is born.

We form our beliefs around alcohol through observation and experience. We watch someone take a shot before walking onto the dance floor. We learn that saying yes to a drink is one way of joining in. We associate cocktails with vacations, romance, success, and relaxation. And then we experience it for ourselves. Conversation flows more easily after a few drinks. The self-conscious voice in our head grows quieter as the alcohol kicks in. A warm rush of pleasure arrives somewhere around the second cocktail.

Somewhere along the line, we form beliefs that sound like:

  • "Alcohol boosts my confidence."
  • "Alcohol helps me connect."
  • "Alcohol makes me happy."

These unexamined beliefs are the second invisible force that fuels an unwanted drinking pattern. When these beliefs remain unexamined and unchallenged, they often continue to fuel the desire to drink even after we decide to quit.

The Near Enemy Trap
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

The 'Near Enemy Trap'

The trickiest part is that these beliefs aren't entirely made up.

The reason that these beliefs around alcohol can feel extremely convincing is that alcohol is very good at giving us something that feels almost like what we want.

  • We want confidence; alcohol hands us liquid courage.
  • We want belonging; alcohol helps us fit in.
  • We want happiness; alcohol gives us pleasure.

Alcohol gives us a taste of what we deeply desire, so much so that we often fall into the illusion that drinking can give us what we need. But what alcohol offers is often subtly different from the real thing. And when we get caught pursuing the imitation, we can end up moving further away—not closer—to what we were seeking in the first place.

There is actually a Buddhist concept that describes this kind of paradox: the “near enemy.” A near enemy is a Buddhist concept referring to something that so closely resembles a quality we want that we can mistake it for the real thing. But a near enemy is subtly different—and can actually lead us away from what we’re seeking.

When it comes to our relationship with alcohol, I call this paradox the Near Enemy Trap.

How to recognize a Near Enemy Trap: Spot the difference

Oftentimes, we continue to miss alcohol after deciding to quit because we are still caught in the Near Enemy Trap—believing that by letting go of alcohol, we are giving up something we need or deeply desire. When alcohol still represents confidence, connection, or happiness, then it’s only natural that giving it up can feel like a loss.

Only when we begin to see the difference between what we truly want and what alcohol actually gives us can we start to question whether we're really giving up as much as we thought.

item.title: The “Divorce Glow-Up” Is Having a Moment
item.description:
Divorce

The “Divorce Glow-Up” Is Having a Moment

What’s behind the "divorce glow-up" filter, and what's wrong with its signaling.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • The "Divorce Glow-Up" is a social media trend showcasing women leveling up after their marriages end.
  • Social media trends can be problematic if accepted as truth without understanding context.
  • Divorce isn’t an instant transition or automatically empowering but an invitation to reflect.
  • Ultimately, the real divorce glow-up can only be the result of a much deeper transformation.
Source: Kaamna Bhojwani/Created with AI

As all cultural movements do in this day and age, this one started on TikTok.

Since the end of 2025, women have been posting their “divorce glow-ups” — before-and-after images and videos showcasing life after ending a marriage. As the term “glow-up” suggests, the “after” is a flex: better bodies, better haircuts. Better them.

And like every TikTok trend worth its salt, this one also spawned a full retail economy in its wake. Divorce-themed Evites. Etsy merch sporting captions like Divorced AF; I Do, I Did, I’m Done; or End of an Error. The Guardian even declared 2026 to be “hot divorcee summer”.

As someone who’s had personal experience with this particular journey, I can tell you that if living in an unfulfilling marriage doesn’t dampen your will to live, the divorce process will. If you are fortunate enough to come out unscathed and inspired to live better, that is indeed something to be celebrated.

But also, as a relationship scientist focused on authentic intimacy, I balk at anything that is performative and simplistic, which is where TikTok trends often reside. If taken as truthful universal experiences, these fleeting trends can cause lasting harm.

The divorce glow-up is no exception. To understand the context behind the content, we must take a look behind the filter.

It's not about looks, it's about energy.

Getting divorced doesn’t make you pretty, psychotherapist Annie Wright rightly declares in USA Today. The divorce glow-up is signaling is an energy reclamation, not a beauty transformation. Living in a toxic relationship, carrying the emotional load of a non-reciprocal partnership, or doubting yourself or the choices you’ve made – these are heavy burdens. The physiological, emotional and mental toll is real.

The divorce glow-up is a nervous system coming off high alert.

It's neither instantaneous nor inevitable.

A 90-second TikTok reel could make you believe that you can go from a bad marriage to a baddie new existence with an up-leveled job, snatched waist and a new lover overnight. The reality is far from it. The metamorphosis takes months, often years, depending on how long you were married and the circumstances under which you left.

Not having a cinematic post-divorce era isn’t a personal failure, but the toxic positivity of this trend can do real damage to those who feel like they’re not on the glow-up timeline, or don't have one at all.

In addition, we have to hold space for the grief that accompanies the loss of a relationship that once was, which this trend wholly ignores.

It's not about toxicity, it's about maturity.

“Dump Him”, reads the signature “Emma” sweatshirt from Reformation’s Divorce Line, created with Laura Wasser, divorce lawyer to the stars. A decade ago, encouraging women to leave their male partners would have been a risky choice for a brand to lean into. Today it signals an acceptance of women shunning relationships that don’t satisfy them, and the elevated status of single, divorced and unmarried women.

But writing off every man, every relationship, and every faux-pas as a red flag is toxic in its own right. Evaluating partners not with a knee-jerk negative reflex but through thoughtful discernment of the self and the other is a sign of maturity. Let this trend not discourage the development of judgment, patience and self-accountability in our intimate relationships.

It's not about leaving men, it's about choosing yourself.

Men don’t get prizes for leaving a relationship. When they do, we’re not particularly surprised, which is troubling in and of itself. But men also don’t tend to face the same pressures to stay as women do. Across the globe, when a woman expresses discontent or disillusionment with her marriage, she is bombarded with a barrage of reasons for why she should willingly forsake herself on this literal and proverbial altar. Societal expectations, marital vows, chidren's wellbeing, familial reputation — all may be put before her own wellbeing.

Overcoming that pressure is a heroic feat. Men aren’t usually told to stick it out and suck it up. Only women are expected to swallow that pill.

It's not about partners, it's about how we partner.

Contrary to popular belief, people still want to get married. Data as recent as April 2026 show that 81% of Gen Z participants say they would like to be married one day. The number of people racing to marry their AI companions suggests that the desire for partnership isn’t dying. What’s dying is our tolerance for partnerships that confuse commitment with an abdication of the self.

For women in particular, society forces us to marry before we are ready, because of our biological clock, or because we're convinced our beauty has a shelf life. We don't wait until we have a solid financial foundation and often choose men who look good on paper but are incompatible with us in every other way that matters.

Marriages may not be becoming obsolete but these power dynamics and cultural norms are shifting. Relationships that don't make the cut are being cut out.

The True Lesson Behind the Trend

Divorce glow ups should not glorify break-ups. They should celebrate reunions – with the self.

Some marriages have to end — abuse and violence are not negotiable, and for those women, leaving is the whole story. Period. There’s nothing more to be said. But many divorces aren’t that. Most divorces come at a choice point. They may be a verdict on the marriage or on the man. But more importantly, they are an invitation to actually look at your own patterns before you build another relationship on the same shaky foundations.

Reclaiming the keys to your kingdom is a flex. Not handing them over in the first place is a win. When you can take the pain and sorrow and grief and disillusionment from the end of a marriage and transmute it into an undying commitment your true self, that’s the real glow-up.

Otherwise it’s just words on a sweatshirt.
